# Phase 2 — Improved Compatibility-First Architecture

The Awtsmoos joins boundless ohr to measured keli, possibility to covenant, motion to form;
Awtsmoos.com should let any future thing arrive without turning every present API into migration storm.

## Stable Core Contract

A resource envelope should contain only universally useful identity and discovery fields:

- `id`
- `type`
- `title`
- `data`
- `schema`
- `links`
- `capabilities`
- `meta`

Everything richer—relationships, actions, history, provenance, jobs, presentation, representations—must be optional capability sections with stable names and version metadata.

## Type Definitions

Type definitions are themselves inspectable resources. Each definition can declare:

- namespaced identifier
- contract version
- lifecycle state
- human labels/descriptions
- schema and semantic field roles
- supported relationships
- supported actions
- queryable/sortable/filterable fields
- available render modes
- compatibility aliases
- documentation/examples
- deprecation/replacement metadata

A type registry does not own domain storage. It describes how existing domain resources participate in Portal interoperability.

## Schema Layer

Do not create a new validator before inspecting existing validators. Define a normalized internal schema vocabulary and adapters from current JSON-schema-like systems. Preserve source-schema identity so clients and tooling can inspect the original dialect when necessary.

Validation always has budgets: depth, object properties, array length, string size, reference count, union branches, and recursion.

## Action Layer

Each action has a stable machine ID plus human presentation metadata. It declares:

- input schema
- output type(s)
- availability/permission hint
- destructive/confirmation policy
- synchronous or job-backed execution
- idempotency/retry behavior
- concurrency/revision preconditions
- dry-run/preview support where real domain behavior permits it

Invocation is separately authorized and validated; descriptors never grant permission by themselves.

## Query + Collection Layer

A collection advertises the operators it genuinely supports. Generic clients build only allowed queries. Backends enforce cost budgets and may return structured unsupported/cost errors rather than pretending every field supports arbitrary traversal.

Collections can describe cursors, totals, facets, sort choices, projection, groups, aggregates, bulk actions, and saved views as capabilities.

## Relationship Layer

Relationships are optional typed links with direction, target type, target identity, label, and navigation URL. Backlinks are provided only when a domain can support them efficiently. Graph visualization is a renderer over relationship-capable resources—not the universal storage model.

## Provenance + History Layer

Revision and provenance are distinct:

- history answers “how did this resource change?”
- provenance answers “where did this value/resource originate?”

Generated or inferred resources can attach transformer/model/tool/source references and confidence/status without implying deterministic reproducibility when none exists.

## Job + Stream Layer

Jobs use a stable state machine and can expose progress stages, logs, output resources, cancellation, retry capability, and parent/child relationships. Streaming events augment snapshots; clients can always recover by re-fetching the canonical resource/job.

## Transformation Layer

A transformer describes accepted types, configuration schema, output types, side-effect class, determinism, execution mode, permission needs, and cost hints. Pipelines compose transformer resources but do not bypass each transformer's validation/security boundary.

## UI Layer

The universal renderer uses a deterministic fallback chain:

1. exact type + view renderer
2. type-family renderer
3. semantic-role renderer
4. schema-based renderer
5. bounded generic object/list renderer
6. explicit developer/raw inspector

Unknown data never becomes an exception merely because no specialized renderer exists.

## Stable Visual Foundation

The shared design foundation initially activates only inside a portal-root scope. It provides:

- type and spacing tokens
- solid surfaces/borders/elevation
- intentional native element styling
- buttons/forms/lists/tables/details/code/media/dialog defaults
- focus-visible/reduced-motion/logical properties
- mobile target sizing, safe areas, `dvh`, overflow rules
- loading/empty/error/status patterns

Specialized apps can inherit foundations without inheriting a visual theme.

## Migration Strategy

Adapters are one-way at first: legacy domain payload → Portal resource envelope. Existing endpoints and consumers remain unchanged. A new discovery surface can expose adapted resources to the generic client. Only after equivalence tests and real adoption should domains optionally return resource envelopes natively.

## Verification Strategy

Every resource contract test includes:

- valid minimal envelope
- maximal optional capabilities
- unknown extension fields
- malformed schema/action/query data
- permission descriptor versus invocation authorization
- recursion/size budget enforcement
- version/deprecation behavior
- serialization stability
- specialized renderer and fallback renderer equivalence on core semantics
- narrow/wide/mobile UI behavior

## NEXT_ACTION

Perform Phase 3 critique with thirty additional operational/evolution/UI hardening improvements, then write the final execution plan before inspecting implementation targets.
